cues.text: Section ten: applied continuity scenarios.
Let us begin with the first scenario, pandemic disruption.
COVID-19 demonstrated that continuity involves more than recovering servers.
Organisations needed remote access, collaboration platforms, secure devices, digital customer channels, staff support and scalable infrastructure.
Think about how this played out in different sectors.
Schools needed remote learning.
Banks needed digital transactions.
Healthcare providers needed secure coordination.
Remote work, however, introduced risks of its own.
These included insecure devices, weak connectivity and increased exposure to phishing.
Appropriate controls include multi-factor authentication, secure access, endpoint management, training and alternative communication channels.
And continuity must account for staff availability and supplier disruption, as well as technology.
A plan that restores systems but ignores whether people can actually work, or whether suppliers can deliver, is incomplete.
Now let us turn to the second scenario, a Nigerian financial services scenario.
Consider a bank experiencing a regional power outage and network disruption.
Its critical functions include payments, customer access and reconciliation.
A continuity strategy could combine independent power sources, diverse connectivity, geographically separated recovery infrastructure and alternative customer support.

Notice how each element answers a specific threat: independent power addresses the outage, diverse connectivity addresses the network disruption, separated recovery infrastructure addresses the loss of a single location, and alternative support keeps customers served while systems are affected.
A tabletop exercise might simulate three conditions: primary-site loss, delayed vendor response and uncertainty about replication status.
Participants then decide when to activate the plan, verify standby health, communicate with stakeholders, reconcile transactions and return to normal operations.
Finally, a useful exercise report records decisions, observed gaps, recovery measurements, owners and deadlines.
The aim is to discover weaknesses before an actual crisis, not to declare success because participants attended a meeting.
